newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa black-owned companies gain investor trust.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa black-owned companies gain investor trust.

text.p: South Africa's small band of black-owned companies are growing in stature and respect in the post-apartheid era after winning significant control of listed companies in 1996, market analysts said on Tuesday.

The number of black-owned companies listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE) grew to 17 by the end of 1996 from 10 by the end of 1995, according to JSE figures. Most have listed in the post-apartheid period
Their market capitalisation grew to 26.5 billion rand ($5.7 billion) by the end of 1996 from 6.5 billion rand in 1995, JSE figures show.

Last year's deal between Anglo American Corporation of South Africa Ltd to sell 35 percent of Johnnies Industrial Corporation (Johnnies) to the National Empowerment Consortium with an option to increase the shareholding to 47.4 was seen as a milestone in black economic empowerment.
It was followed shortly afterwards by Anglo's sale of a similar stake in JCI to another black consortium lead by Capital Alliance Holdings Ltd.

"The process of (blacks) taking a rightful share of the economy is growing rapidly. Economic empowerment as a movement is growing fast in South Africa," Leon van Heerden, analyst at BOE Natwest, told Reuters.
A share dealer who declined to be identified said: "Investors were rather sceptical but as earnings started to come through and also acquisitions...they have overcome their initial scepticism."

The head of research at another South African brokerage said a portfolio of black-owned companies weighted for market capitalisation and held from August 1995 to August 1996 would have appreciated by some 90 percent. Returns for an unweighted portfolio would have been 55 percent.
Van Heerden said one of the reasons for this strong growth was that black companies tended to favour the financial sector.
"One of the reasons for their overall growth is they have a strong holding in financial services and life assurance companies which generally outperform the overall index," he said.

But black companies also have two extra levers with which to add value -- firstly by being able to negotiate acquisitions at a discount from sellers eager to promote black empowerment and secondly through winning government contracts and tenders most of which require a partnership with black-owned companies.

"In several cases they have been able to do deals at a discount. The ability to obtain assets at a discount adds value...and certainly on government tenders and contracts where a company has to have a black partner they will be able to add value," the head of research said.
Black-owned companies have been growing in stature but analysts said it remained to be seen how they would spread economic empowerment to the wider black population.
"A number of people are being enriched. To what extent that will start to have an impact on affirmative action and reconstruction within the companies remains to be seen," the head of research said.
JSE figures show Johnnies and JCI as the biggest black-owned concerns on the stock market with market capitalisations of 7.84 billion rand and 7.01 billion respectively at the end of 1996.
Other black firms topping the one billion rand mark are Metropolitan Life (4.50 billion), Capital Alliance (1.93 billion), African Life Assurance (1.37 billion) and Real Africa Investments.
